title: Isandro and the Hymn
premise: Noor Montrose, a property surveyor with a decade of rationalizations behind them, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House, a derelict estate where every mirror lags one second behind reality. The lag is a countdown: the house's original owners drowned a child in the well in 1974 and stole her voice, which has been singing through the pipes ever since, and the mirrors are the house's eyes learning to see Noor. As Noor digs into the town's complicity, they discover their own family took something from the house too, and the well is refilling with everything it was denied. To survive, Noor must return the stolen voice to the well on the night it refills, choosing truth over the loyalty that kept their family's secret for fifty years, and the house finally lets them go, though the mirrors everywhere now lag for Noor alone.
about_author: Mara Nystrom is the pen name of a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent years cataloguing houses no one wanted to buy. Their fiction blends survey reports, folklore, and the quiet dread of old architecture.

chapters.title: The Lag
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Arriving at Hollowmere House for a routine appraisal, Noor notices a mirror showing the room a beat behind. They blame a trick of light, but the beat repeats in every reflective surface. Emotional beat: the first crack in ten years of rationalization.

chapters.title: Inventory of Wrong Rooms
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Measuring the house, Noor finds rooms whose dimensions don't match the blueprints, as if the house has grown around something. A pipe hums a melody Noor almost recognizes. Emotional beat: professional detachment curdling into unease.

chapters.title: What the Deed Says
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In the county archive, Noor finds the deed history: the Halloway family bought the house in 1946 and every record after 1974 is signed by the same dead hand. Emotional beat: the thrill of a paper trail becoming dread.

chapters.title: The Hymn in the Pipes
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Night one in the house. The plumbing sings a child's hymn; Noor records it and the recording plays back with a second voice underneath. Emotional beat: loneliness giving way to a sense of being accompanied.

chapters.title: Aunt Vess's Silence
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, with phone-call interludes. Noor calls their aunt, who grew up nearby; Vess goes quiet at the house's name and says only: 'Don't count the mirrors.' Emotional beat: loyalty's first visible cost.

chapters.title: 1974, According to the Town
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In the library's newspaper mircrofilm, Noor finds a drowned girl, Edith Halloway, age nine, ruled accidental. The article's photo shows the hymn's sheet music in her hands. Emotional beat: grief for a stranger.

chapters.title: Reflections That Watch Back
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The lag lengthens to two seconds. In one mirror, Noor sees themselves turn to look at the stairs after Noor has already looked away. Emotional beat: the observer becoming the observed.

chapters.title: The Well Refills Slowly
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor finds the sealed wellhouse; the water level rises visibly, carrying things up from below: a shoe, a hymnal, a child's dental records. Emotional beat: the past surfacing, literally.

chapters.title: Vess Comes to the House
chapters.summary: Vess's POV. Aunt Vess arrives uninvited, begging Noor to leave. She admits she was Edith's playmate and that the town's children were told never to sing the hymn aloud. Emotional beat: love expressed as obstruction.

chapters.title: What Our Family Took
chapters.summary: Vess's POV, continuing. Vess confesses: Noor's grandfather, the town's surveyor, falsified the 1974 report and kept Edith's voice, recorded on a wire spool, as 'evidence' he never surrendered. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as theft.

chapters.title: The Wire Spool
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In their grandfather's old survey kit, kept in the attic of the house, Noor finds the spool. Playing it, they hear Edith singing, then screaming, then a man's voice saying 'that's enough now.' Emotional beat: horror at one's own blood.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The house begins evaluating Noor: doors open onto accurate measurements of Noor's life, rooms furnished with their memories. The mirrors now lag three seconds. Emotional beat: being known is worse than being haunted.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor confronts Vess: why keep the secret? Vess says the town agreed silence protected everyone, and that the grandfather believed he was containing something dangerous. Emotional beat: the theme of loyalty vs. truth made explicit and unresolved.

chapters.title: The Second Voice on the Tape
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Replaying the spool slowed, Noor hears a second voice beneath Edith's: older, wet, singing the harmony. The well was not empty in 1974. Emotional beat: the horror deepens past the crime to the thing the crime fed.

chapters.title: Neighbors at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Townspeople appear at the property line, watching the house, some holding hymnals. They don't threaten; they wait. One whispers: 'It's almost full.' Emotional beat: communal complicity as quiet menace.

chapters.title: The Lag Reaches Five
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The mirrors now show Noor things that haven't happened yet: Noor walking into the wellhouse, then not walking out. Emotional beat: fatalism versus the choice to act anyway.

chapters.title: Vess's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vess's POV. Vess returns with the town's offer: give back the spool, but never speak of what's in the well, and Noor can live. Noor refuses, because silence is how Edith stayed drowned twice. Emotional beat: Noor choosing truth, breaking the family pattern.

chapters.title: Night of the Refill
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. On the anniversary, the well brims. The house's mirrors all show the wellhouse, lagging, waiting. Noor carries the spool across the grounds while the hymn swells from every pipe at once. Emotional beat: terrified resolve.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, climax. At the well's edge, the second voice rises to meet Noor, wearing the reflection of everyone Noor has betrayed or lost. Noor names the family's crime aloud, drops the spool into the water, and the well takes the voice back, screaming, singing, then silent. Emotional beat: sacrifice and reckoning.

chapters.title: The House Lets Go
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Dawn. The mirrors reflect in real time. The rooms match their blueprints. Edith's presence is gone, and with it the second voice, which the well has finally digested. Emotional beat: exhausted relief shadowed by what was fed to buy it.

chapters.title: Appraisal Complete
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor files the true report: the house's history, the crime, the town's silence, over Vess's anguished objections. The town turns on them; Vess does not call again. Emotional beat: the cost of truth paid in full.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, coda. Months later, in a city apartment, Noor catches their own reflection lagging by a single second. It doesn't follow them. It just watches, and once, faintly, hums. Emotional beat: ambiguous peace, memory as the haunting that never fully drains.
